title: Speeding up Automated Algorithm Design by Batch Evaluation: A Case Study of Genetic Programming for Ant Colony Optimisation
summary:
arXiv:2611.19751v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluation is becoming the bottleneck of automated algorithm design, especially for iterative algorithms such as ant colony optimisation (ACO), which must run to completion on multiple instances. A transition rule designed by genetic programming reads the construction state of each ant and must be evaluated at every step. However, existing GPU methods for ACO precompute a fixed rule and parallelise the ants of one run. To address this issue, we propose BlockEval, a batch evaluation framework with GPU and CPU backends. The GPU backend executes many runs simultaneously, each as a whole in one thread block, and compiles one module per generation. When an ant has visited all its candidate cities, a warp-cooperative fallback stalls only its warp where possible. On travelling salesman problems with 50--1000 cities, the GPU backend is 4.1--16.5 times faster than the CPU backend on 32 cores and 11.2--17.8 times faster than EvoGP+TensorACO-CL.

title: Shortcut Learning in Feature-Based Algorithm Selection
summary:
arXiv:2611.20440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Landscape features give learning models information about the objective function for algorithm selection, algorithm configuration, and performance prediction. Should these features capture more information? Not always, because a model may rely on information that the algorithms ignore. This phenomenon is called shortcut learning, and in-distribution accuracy can hide it. We propose the Rubber Ruler Test. It transforms the objective values of test instances with random strictly increasing transformations, reruns the algorithms, and measures prediction performance. Comparison-based algorithms such as CMA-ES perform identically after the transformation, so for them any drop reveals shortcut learning. On 10-dimensional BBOB, a model for two comparison-based algorithms learned shortcuts even from normalized objective values. The R^2 of a model using all ELA features dropped from 0.85 to 0.23, below 0.45 with invariant features only. Rank-based features reduced the drop when algorithms search using ranks. Data augmentation with transformed training instances improved prediction on transformed instances for every portfolio we studied, but lowered R^2 on original instances by up to 0.31. These results suggest that models should rely only on information that the algorithms use. We recommend reporting the Rubber Ruler Test alongside in-distribution accuracy and using it to choose feature extraction and data augmentation.

title: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification
summary:
arXiv:2611.18657v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Complete formal verification of neural networks is crucial for their deployment in safety-critical domains. A key bottleneck stems from encoding complexity: traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron. We propose the Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART), which fundamentally breaks the conventional one-to-one mapping between unstable neurons and binary variables by establishing formal reducibility criteria. This allows for finer-grained modeling, where each unstable neuron corresponds on average to fewer than one binary variable, thereby reducing verification complexity at its source. Based on SART, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the number of binary variables required for complete verification and, under the assumption that $P \neq NP$, prove that variables in the final layer can be compressed by 50\%, while the number of variables in intermediate layers cannot be further reduced. To overcome the apparent ``last-layer-only'' limitation, we recast verification as a sequential process and, crucially, show that the gain lifts to the entire network: LayerABS, a SART-based progressive tightening verifier, iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers and propagates tight bounds that shrink the global search space and binary-variable counts. Furthermore, we reveal a structural law influencing verification complexity: when the signs of weights of unstable neurons satisfy numerical symmetry, with positive and negative weights equal or differing by at most one, the worst-case verification complexity achieves the theoretical optimum, offering theoretical guidance for the design of verification-friendly architectures. As a general-purpose underlying encoding, the value of SART is independent of specific algorithms.

title: Simulated Annealing with Topological Spatial Chunking for De Novo Protein Sequence Design
summary:
arXiv:2611.19158v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The inverse protein folding problem, designing a discrete amino acid sequence that spontaneously folds into a predefined macroscopic structure, remains a phenomenally demanding combinatorial challenge central to synthetic drug discovery. While algorithms like SA offer a baseline approach for navigating dense biomolecular energy landscapes, applying SA heuristics to large sequences is inherently frustrated by exponentially large search spaces and deep local energy minima. This study proposes a scalable sequence design architecture, Topological Spatial Chunking Simulated Annealing, based on a localized, exact-solving heuristic embedded within a global simulated-annealing wrapper. To fundamentally circumvent exponential scaling walls, we deploy a dynamic solver that segments the global molecular target into shallow, k-variable algorithmic windows. Crucially, rather than partitioning natively by sequential 1D chronology, we introduce topological spatial chunking, which dynamically groups discrete variables based on Euclidean spatial proximity to preserve critical non-local thermodynamic correlations. The spatially localized sub-problems are solved deterministically via exact enumeration, while the global traversal is securely regulated by an exterior simulated annealing governor augmented by dynamic reheating and continuous elitism caching. We comprehensively benchmarked this classical architecture on the standard HP biophysical lattice against targeted 20-merA, 25-mer, 50-mer, and 64-mer geometries. Most notably, when evaluating the computationally exhaustive 50-mer and 64-mer topologies, the framework successfully bypassed widely accepted heuristic boundaries. By leveraging deterministic exact solving to vault classical energy traps, the system algorithmically resolved a novel, ultra-dense sequence-packing configuration for the 50-mer, defining a new theoretical global optimum.

title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
summary:
arXiv:2611.19597v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints.
  We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure.
  NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents
summary:
arXiv:2611.21056v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
summary:
arXiv:2611.21598v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
summary:
arXiv:2610.16102v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tacit knowing is an operating regime of memory, not a separate content. In VaCoAl (CASRAM, PyVaCoAl), a deterministic hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With all collisions repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks any; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path confidence $CR_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes unstated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to is non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is contingent or regime-bound, putting Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The lemma answers the popular dual-process moral ("train slow System 2 to tame fast System 1"), mirroring the two-store reading of knowledge Polanyi rejected; Mercier and Sperber's reasoning as intuitive inference about reasons matches his. (4) To know a large DAG is to cull it. Against Polanyi's Meno reading, Simon held that a test and a generator, guided by statable heuristics, suffice. The AlphaGo-to-AlphaProof lineage builds the test, but its strongest systems cull by unstatable valuations: the tacit is relocated, not removed, results are verified yet rootless, and practicable traces must record the cull. (5) Collins's three tacit knowledges are bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (6) Our mentor-student DAG maps tacit transmission. (7) AI-solved problems lacking follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted if LLMs generate, VaCoAl traces, the community values. (8) For Mercier and Sperber an LLM is a sophist; truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, conjectured to extend beyond humans; machine-only knowledge reaches at most Sosa's animal grade. Testable predictions follow.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary:
arXiv:2610.41291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3 to 194.9 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
summary:
arXiv:2611.16013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$) CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
summary:
arXiv:2611.16057v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.
